Choosing the inner tuner

Source: vignettes/tuners.Rmd
tuners.Rmd

The inner search of a nested run can use a fixed grid, a race, Bayesian optimization or simulated annealing. Each search has a nested function that takes the same design and workflow and returns the same kind of result. A race spends fewer fits when some candidates (settings tried) are clearly worse. The Bayesian and annealing searches propose candidates from ranges rather than a fixed grid.

vignette("nested-cv") uses the grid. This page runs the other searches on the same example. It then scores two more things on the same folds: a workflow with nothing to tune, and a set of workflows.

library(tidymodels)
library(nestedtune)

The setup

We reuse the design, the random forest and the grid from vignette("nested-cv").

set.seed(1)

folds <- nested_resamples(
  mtcars,
  outside = vfold_cv(v = 5),
  inside = vfold_cv(v = 5)
)

rf <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("regression")

wf <- workflow(mpg ~ ., rf)

grid <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2L, 5L, 8L), min_n = c(2L, 10L))

The Bayesian and annealing searches propose their own candidates from a range for each parameter. tune_bayes() does not accept a range that depends on the data, such as that of mtry, so we set it by hand. We also keep min_n within the grid’s range, because its default range is larger than an inner analysis set here.

params <- update(
  extract_parameter_set_dials(wf),
  mtry = mtry(c(2L, 8L)),
  min_n = min_n(c(2L, 10L))
)

Bayesian optimization

nested_tune_bayes() runs tune::tune_bayes() in each outer fold. The search scores initial starting candidates, then proposes iter more, one at a time, from a Gaussian process model of the scores so far. We keep both small so the page builds quickly.

set.seed(2)

bayes <- nested_tune_bayes(
  wf,
  folds,
  param_info = params,
  initial = 4,
  iter = 3
)

bayes
#> 
#> ── Nested cross-validation results ────────────────────────────────────
#> Outer resamples: 5-fold cross-validation
#> # A tibble: 5 × 9
#>   splits         id    .metrics .selected .inner_metrics    .notes  
#>   <list>         <chr> <list>   <list>    <list>            <list>  
#> 1 <split [25/7]> Fold1 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [14 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 2 <split [25/7]> Fold2 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [14 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 3 <split [26/6]> Fold3 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [14 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 4 <split [26/6]> Fold4 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [14 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 5 <split [26/6]> Fold5 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [14 × 9]> <tibble>
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: .completed <lgl>, .tuning_seed <int>,
#> #   .outer_fit_seed <int>
#> ! Candidates searched: 7, 7, 7, 7, 7. The folds did not search the
#>   same grid
#> ℹ Use `summary()` for what the run means: which folds failed, what
#>   each one selected, and the estimate across them.

Each fold proposes candidates from its own scores, so the folds do not search the same set, and the print says so.

Racing

The racing functions take a grid. They score every candidate on a few inner resamples first, and then stop scoring the candidates that are clearly worse than the best. nested_tune_race_anova() decides with an ANOVA model, and nested_tune_race_win_loss() decides with a model of pairwise wins.

set.seed(3)

race <- nested_tune_race_anova(wf, folds, grid = grid)

race
#> 
#> ── Nested cross-validation results ────────────────────────────────────
#> Outer resamples: 5-fold cross-validation
#> # A tibble: 5 × 9
#>   splits         id    .metrics .selected .inner_metrics    .notes  
#>   <list>         <chr> <list>   <list>    <list>            <list>  
#> 1 <split [25/7]> Fold1 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 8]> <tibble>
#> 2 <split [25/7]> Fold2 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 8]> <tibble>
#> 3 <split [26/6]> Fold3 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 8]> <tibble>
#> 4 <split [26/6]> Fold4 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 8]> <tibble>
#> 5 <split [26/6]> Fold5 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 8]> <tibble>
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: .completed <lgl>, .tuning_seed <int>,
#> #   .outer_fit_seed <int>
#> ℹ Use `summary()` for what the run means: which folds failed, what
#>   each one selected, and the estimate across them.

The inner metrics show how many resamples scored each candidate. Summed over one metric, they give the fits each fold spent on tuning. A full grid search costs 30 fits per fold.

collect_inner_metrics(race) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(fits = sum(n))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   id     fits
#>   <chr> <int>
#> 1 Fold1    30
#> 2 Fold2    30
#> 3 Fold3    23
#> 4 Fold4    29
#> 5 Fold5    30

On this small example the race dropped few candidates. The win/loss race is called the same way. Here are its fits per fold.

set.seed(4)

win_loss <- nested_tune_race_win_loss(wf, folds, grid = grid)

collect_inner_metrics(win_loss) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarise(fits = sum(n))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>   id     fits
#>   <chr> <int>
#> 1 Fold1    30
#> 2 Fold2    30
#> 3 Fold3    30
#> 4 Fold4    28
#> 5 Fold5    30

Simulated annealing

nested_tune_sim_anneal() runs finetune::tune_sim_anneal() in each outer fold. Each proposal is a small random move from the current candidate. It is kept when it scores better, and sometimes when it scores worse. The control below turns off finetune’s log of every move.

set.seed(5)

anneal <- nested_tune_sim_anneal(
  wf,
  folds,
  param_info = params,
  initial = 3,
  iter = 3,
  control = finetune::control_sim_anneal(verbose_iter = FALSE)
)

anneal
#> 
#> ── Nested cross-validation results ────────────────────────────────────
#> Outer resamples: 5-fold cross-validation
#> # A tibble: 5 × 9
#>   splits         id    .metrics .selected .inner_metrics    .notes  
#>   <list>         <chr> <list>   <list>    <list>            <list>  
#> 1 <split [25/7]> Fold1 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 2 <split [25/7]> Fold2 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 3 <split [26/6]> Fold3 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 4 <split [26/6]> Fold4 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 9]> <tibble>
#> 5 <split [26/6]> Fold5 <tibble> <tibble>  <tibble [12 × 9]> <tibble>
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: .completed <lgl>, .tuning_seed <int>,
#> #   .outer_fit_seed <int>
#> ! Candidates searched: 6, 6, 6, 6, 6. The folds did not search the
#>   same grid
#> ℹ Use `summary()` for what the run means: which folds failed, what
#>   each one selected, and the estimate across them.

A workflow with nothing to tune

A tuned model is often compared with the same model at fixed settings, here one of the grid’s. nested_fit_resamples() scores such a workflow on the same nested design. Each outer fold fits the workflow on its analysis rows and scores it on its assessment rows.

fixed_rf <- rand_forest(mtry = 2L, min_n = 10L, trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger") |>
  set_mode("regression")

set.seed(2)
baseline <- nested_fit_resamples(workflow(mpg ~ ., fixed_rf), folds)

collect_metrics(baseline)
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   .metric .estimator  mean     n std_err
#>   <chr>   <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 rmse    standard   2.75      5  0.576 
#> 2 rsq     standard   0.827     5  0.0274

Both runs used the same folds, so we can join their scores fold by fold.

collect_metrics(bayes, summarize = FALSE) |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  select(id, tuned = .estimate) |>
  left_join(
    collect_metrics(baseline, summarize = FALSE) |>
      filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
      select(id, fixed = .estimate),
    by = "id"
  )
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   id    tuned fixed
#>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Fold1  1.23  1.83
#> 2 Fold2  3.33  3.85
#> 3 Fold3  2.49  1.81
#> 4 Fold4  1.79  1.82
#> 5 Fold5  3.71  4.43

Each row compares the two runs on one fold. A difference between their two nested estimates is not a test, as vignette("estimate") explains.

A set of workflows

nested_workflow_map() runs every workflow of a workflow_set() through one nested function on one design. Our set holds the random forest, a linear model with nothing to tune, and a linear model on a tuned number of principal components. The components workflow takes its own grid through option_add(), which overrides the call’s grid for that workflow alone.

pca <- recipe(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars) |>
  step_normalize(all_predictors()) |>
  step_pca(all_predictors(), num_comp = tune())

wset <- as_workflow_set(
  forest = wf,
  linear = workflow(mpg ~ ., linear_reg()),
  components = workflow(pca, linear_reg())
) |>
  option_add(grid = tibble(num_comp = 1:4), id = "components")

set.seed(7)
mapped <- nested_workflow_map(
  wset,
  fn = "nested_tune_grid",
  resamples = folds,
  grid = grid
)

mapped
#> 
#> ── Nested cross-validation results for a workflow set ─────────────────
#> Orchestrator: `nested_tune_grid()` (grid search)
#> Workflows: 3
#> ✔ "forest": 5 of 5 outer folds completed (grid search)
#> ✔ "linear": 5 of 5 outer folds completed (no tuning)
#> ✔ "components": 5 of 5 outer folds completed (grid search)
#> ℹ Use `collect_metrics()` for every workflow's estimate under its id,
#>   and `x$result[[i]]` for one workflow's run.

The linear model has nothing to tune, so it ran through nested_fit_resamples(), and the print marks it “no tuning”. The collect functions stack their tables under each workflow’s id.

collect_metrics(mapped)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 6
#>   wflow_id   .metric .estimator  mean     n std_err
#>   <chr>      <chr>   <chr>      <dbl> <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 forest     rmse    standard   2.43      5  0.455 
#> 2 forest     rsq     standard   0.847     5  0.0265
#> 3 linear     rmse    standard   4.42      5  0.571 
#> 4 linear     rsq     standard   0.639     5  0.0859
#> 5 components rmse    standard   2.48      5  0.337 
#> 6 components rsq     standard   0.835     5  0.0440

autoplot() puts the workflows side by side, one point per outer fold.

autoplot(mapped, type = "performance")

Picking the best workflow by these estimates is a selection that no outer loop scored. For a workflow chosen in advance, nested_final_fit(mapped, id = "forest") fits the model to deploy, and its rows in collect_metrics(mapped) are the numbers to report.
